title: Unit Group Topology from Neumann Series
description: The unit group of a complete normed ring is open and inversion is locally bounded, proved as corollaries of the Neumann series perturbation theorem. Includes quantitative bounds via explicit series representations.

meta.author: Kato (1966), Rudin (1991)
meta.assumptions: 0 axioms, 0 sorries. All results proved from Mathlib and parent Neumann series theorems.
originalContributions: Perturbation of units: B near A (unit) implies B is a unit
Open ball B(1,1) consists entirely of units
Neumann series representation of perturbed inverses
Quantitative norm bounds on perturbed inverses
Local boundedness of inversion near identity
Left and right inverse identities near 1

overview.historicalContext: The openness of the unit group in a Banach algebra is a fundamental result in functional analysis, first established rigorously by Gel'fand (1941). The proof relies on the Neumann series — the operator-theoretic generalization of the geometric series. Kato's perturbation theory (1966) systematically develops the consequences: if A is invertible and B is close enough to A, the Neumann series for A⁻¹(A-B) converges, giving an explicit inverse for B. This result underpins spectral theory, resolvent calculus, and numerical stability analysis.
overview.problemStatement: Prove that the unit group of a complete normed ring is open and the inversion map is locally bounded, as corollaries of the Neumann series perturbation theorem.
overview.text: Unit group topology: openness of invertible elements and local boundedness of inversion in complete normed rings.
overview.proofStrategy: All results follow from the perturbation theorem `invertible_near_one` (from OQ-02): if ‖1 - B‖ < 1 then B is a unit. For a general unit A, write B = A(1 - A⁻¹(A-B)) and bound ‖A⁻¹(A-B)‖ ≤ ‖A⁻¹‖‖A-B‖ < 1. Norm bounds come from the Neumann series: ‖B⁻¹‖ ≤ (1 - ‖1-B‖)⁻¹.
keyInsights: The unit group is open with explicit radius: B(A, ‖A⁻¹‖⁻¹) consists of units
Perturbed inverses have Neumann series representations: B⁻¹ = ∑(1-B)^n near 1
The proof is purely algebraic + metric — works in any complete normed ring
